page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.e4.4xlarge is a shared-core virtual server built on the x86_64 architecture using KVM virtualization. It features an Intel Xeon E5-2682 v4 processor running at 2.5 GHz, providing 16 shared vCPUs across 8 physical cores with 2 threads per core. Memory capacity is 128.0 GB, delivering an 8:1 memory-to-core allocation (8.0 GB per vCPU). The instance includes no local storage, relying on network-attached volumes, and has no integrated GPU accelerators. Baseline network throughput is configured at 2 Gbps.

Benchmark measurements indicate a pronounced contrast between single-core and parallel execution. In stress-ng testing, single-core CPU throughput ranks in the bottom 10% (952.68), and single-threaded gzip compression is weak (21.32 GB/sec). Conversely, aggregate multi-threaded operations scale to average performance tiers, reflected by a stress-ng multi-core score of 12,852.77, a PassMark CPU score of 15,791.21, and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression at 58.04 GB/sec. Large uncached memory reads achieve 47.92 GB/sec, while write operations reach 34.59 GB/sec. Redis SET throughput registers at 14.78 million operations per second.

Because the ecs.e4.4xlarge uses shared CPU allocations on a legacy processor platform, it offers an economical trade-off prioritizing high RAM capacity over per-thread processing speed. Workloads sensitive to single-threaded latency or requiring modern instructions like AVX-512 will experience limitations. This instance is best suited for memory-intensive caching layers, in-memory databases, batch data processing, and distributed services where high RAM density is primary and compute demands are parallelized.
description: Alibaba Cloud ecs.e4.4xlarge is a memory-oriented, shared-allocation virtual instance powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2682 v4 processor at 2.5 GHz. It provides 16 vCPUs (8 physical cores, 2 threads per core) on the x86_64 architecture, paired with 128.0 GB of RAM. The instance lacks local storage and discrete GPUs, operating on a 2 Gbps baseline network. Benchmark results highlight modest single-core throughput alongside average multi-core and memory subsystem capacity, achieving 14.78 million Redis SET operations per second and a PassMark CPU score of 15,791.21. Due to its shared vCPU model and high memory-to-core ratio of 8.0 GB per vCPU, it functions primarily as a budget-conscious option for memory-heavy, multithreaded enterprise tasks such as in-memory caches, backend batch processing, and non-latency-critical databases.
